elements.old: The fee is not the clever part. The feedback loop is — the bin tells you what you did, every single time.
elements.new: New York · composting required · fines from $25 to $300 · bins are not weighed · no rewards

movedToNotes: Bag fees started nationwide in 1995: you buy official priced bags for general trash, meaning anything that is not recycling or food waste. Food waste is charged by weight at a shared bin.
About ₩490 for a standard bag; fines up to ₩100,000.

How the bin works (now drawn by the 3D diagram): tap the household RFID card, the lid opens, the bin weighs what you drop in, and the household is billed for that weight. 4.2 kg is only an example value.
RFID card: a chip card the bin reads, like a building key fob.
Reward (now on screen): households that cut food waste 10 to 30% against the same period last year earn up to 5,000 points (about ₩5,000).
Separated food waste is turned into animal feed, compost and biogas.

Say: "Trash went down 8% in 1995 and 11% by 1996." Caveat on the 8%: Seoul Solution says the 1995 drop may be overstated because many large items were thrown out free that year, so 1996 (11%) is the more reliable number.

Seoul's bin shows each household how much food waste it threw out each time, and New York has nothing like that yet. This becomes recommendation 1 on slide 19, which also has the 2.4% New York organics figure.

New York line on screen: composting is required and buildings can be fined. The bins do not weigh the food waste and there are no rewards. DSNY fines: $25, $50, $100 for buildings of 1 to 8 units; $100, $200, $300 for 9 or more units.
Transition to Nanjido: this system came after Seoul had already built a garbage mountain.

headline: From Landfill to Park

elements.old: Two mounds, ~90 m high. No gas or leachate treatment existed in Korea at the time.
Energy Dream Center opens on site
elements.new: Energy Dream Center opens on site

elements.old: New York did the same thing.

elements.new:
Once the world's largest landfill

movedToNotes: Nanjido (nahn-jee-doh), Haneul (hah-nool), Noeul (no-ool).
Nanjido was a Han River island, chosen in 1978 because it was easy to reach and far from downtown.
Trash was piled into two mounds about 90 m high (the 3D diagram shows the height, the cap, the gas wells and Haneul Park).
Korea had no modern landfill gas or leachate treatment at the time, so the site gave off methane and toxic gases. Leachate is the dirty liquid that drains out of buried trash.
Planning started in 1991. The dump closed in 1993 and the ground was stabilized. Construction ran 1996 to 2002, in time for the 2002 World Cup.
If asked: some sources say dumping ended in 1992. 1978 to 1993 is the range most sources use.
Landfill gas is now captured and used; the mounds became Haneul (Sky) Park and Noeul Park.
2012: the Energy Dream Center from slide 10 was built on this same ground.
New York is doing the same thing at Freshkills, on roughly the same timeline. Present it as a fair comparison between peers, without lecturing.
Transition: this is the success story; the next slide is what went wrong in 2026.

elements.old: A ban without infrastructure is not a policy. It is a deadline.

elements.old: About 63% of NYC buildings are projected to miss their 2030 LL97 caps. Are we making the same mistake?
elements.new: Discussion: can New York's retrofit workers and supply chain keep up with LL97?

movedToNotes: Gyeonggi (gyung-gee), Cheonan (chuh-nahn), Cheongju (chung-joo), Sejong (seh-jong).
Change of tone: everything before this slide was the success story.
The ban was passed in 2021 with a five-year grace period, and the local governments of Seoul, Incheon and Gyeonggi mostly did not add incinerator capacity during those five years.
The ban started on schedule on January 1, 2026, with no emergency delay.
Direct landfilling means burying raw household trash. Under the ban it has to be burned or processed first.
Public incinerators took on only 80 t more, so much of the waste went to private companies instead, and some of it left the region.
The 1,921 to 2,001 t figures come with no time period, so do not do math between them and the 457 t a day. If someone asks, say the report does not give a period.
Seoul's four incinerators: Gangnam, Mapo, Nowon, Yangcheon.

Where it goes (now drawn on the map diagram): Gangdong ships to private incinerators in Cheonan and Sejong; Gangnam plans to send waste to Cheongju. The map shows straight-line distances (Cheonan about 85 km, Cheongju about 110, Sejong about 125). The 130 km figure is the road distance reported by Seoul Economic Daily, Oct 2026.
Capital region means Seoul, Incheon and Gyeonggi together.
This is an environmental justice issue, because the trash now goes to other cities that did not produce it.
Pending: amendments to the Wastes Control Act, timing unclear. Seongnam is building a 500 t/day replacement incinerator.
Seoul banned direct landfilling of household waste before it built enough incinerators to replace it.
LL97 fines buildings that cannot comply. Ask the question on screen: "Can New York's retrofit workers and supply chain keep up with LL97?" Then stop and wait for answers.

headline: Restoring Cheonggyecheon

elements.old: Stream culverted beneath a double-deck road
Open water, planting, and a walkable corridor
cooler than a parallel road four blocks away
elements.new: cooler than a parallel road 4 to 7 blocks away

elements.old: The gridlock everyone predicted never arrived.
elements.new: Highway carried about 168,000 vehicles a day · predicted gridlock did not happen

elements.old:
Reduced demand is empirically documented, not theoretical. That is exactly the evidence
New York's BQE, Cross Bronx and Gowanus debates are missing.
elements.new:
Reduced demand · fewer car trips when road space is removed
New York highway debates: Brooklyn-Queens Expressway (BQE), Cross Bronx Expressway, Gowanus Expressway

movedToNotes: Say Cheonggyecheon roughly as chung-gyeh-chun. Project facts: 2003 to 2005, about US$281 million, 5.8 km (3.6 miles) of restored corridor. The elevated highway carried about 168,000 vehicles a day and the stream was buried under it. Say these at the headline, since the 168,000 now appears on screen only at the last beat.
Before and after captions now live in the 3D diagram (elevated highway and buried stream, then the opened stream with planted banks and walkways).
The often quoted 639% comes from an overall index, so it cannot be read as a species count. Give the counts for each group instead (plants alone went up about 397%).
µg/m³ means micrograms of particles per cubic meter of air.

The slide shows the biggest estimate (LAF). Say: "That's the highest estimate. Other studies find a smaller effect." WWF found 3 to 4°C cooler than areas 400 m away. A peer-reviewed study that pulled many studies together, the most careful source, found cooler daily average temperatures within about 300 m of the stream.
Corridor bus ridership rose 15.1% (2003 to 2008), but the 2004 bus reform happened at the same time, so do not give the stream all the credit.

Reduced demand: when road space is taken away, some car trips stop happening and nearby streets do not jam as people feared. People arguing about the BQE, Cross Bronx and Gowanus can point to this case.
Transition: Seoul kept going, from one stream to a citywide plan for green space.
